content: The WHO guidelines for leprosy were developed with input from individuals involved in policy formulation and clinicians managing leprosy, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The process involved several groups, each with specific roles and responsibilities. WHO Steering Group The WHO Steering Group comprised staff with expertise in leprosy, disease control, intellectual property, evaluation of essential medicines, neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) management, and gender, equity, and human rights. This group contributed to the development of key questions, provided input during the planning process, and reviewed draft documents, including the planning proposal, literature reviews, and draft guidelines. Guidelines Development Group (GDG) The GDG was tasked with reviewing evidence from systematic reviews and developing recommendations. Members included clinicians with expertise in leprosy diagnosis and management, individuals affected by leprosy, representatives from civil society and NGOs, and experts in programmatic management and implementation of leprosy interventions. Efforts were made to ensure diversity in gender, geographical representation, and intellectual perspectives. Given the high burden of leprosy in the WHO South-East Asia Region, representation from this region was prioritized. The GDG met twice: in New Delhi, India, on May 30–31, 2017, and via teleconference on October 27, 2017. The second meeting reviewed additional evidence published in August 2017 on leprosy treatment. Recommendations were developed through discussion and consensus, with all recommendations being unanimous. Systematic Review Team The WHO Secretariat commissioned systematic reviews on leprosy diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. The review team was led by Dr. Amudha Poobalan from the Institute of Applied Health Sciences, Aberdeen University, United Kingdom. External Review Group (ERG) The ERG consisted of experts in leprosy and health program implementation. Their role was to identify errors or missing data, comment on clarity, and highlight issues and implications for implementation. However, they did not modify the recommendations agreed upon by the GDG. Members were selected after the May 2017 GDG meeting, ensuring regional and gender balance and representation of various areas of expertise, including clinical, public health, and social sciences. A Declaration of Interest form was collected from all ERG members. The ERG included individuals from the ILEP Panel of Women and Men Affected by Leprosy, representing five countries (Brazil, Ghana, India, Nepal, and Paraguay). Reviewers disclosed conflicts of interest, but their involvement in the recommendation formulation process was limited, ensuring impartiality. Guidelines Methodologist The methodologist oversaw the collection and grading of evidence and facilitated discussions during GDG meetings, acting as vice-chair. Professor Roger Chou from Oregon Health and Science University, USA, served as the methodologist for these guidelines. External Partners Key partner organizations involved in the review and dissemination of the guidelines included ILEP and its 14 member NGOs, the Nippon Foundation, and the Sasakawa Memorial Health Foundation. These organizations have been major donors to the Global Leprosy Programme (GLP) for many years. Three staff members from these organizations attended the GDG meetings as observers, without participating in the formulation of recommendations. Management of Conflicts of Interest Managing conflicts of interest was a critical aspect of the guideline development process. All potential GDG and ERG members submitted a Declaration of Interest form before their appointment. The GLP Team Leader and the WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics reviewed these declarations and sought clarifications when necessary. Conflicts were assessed to determine whether exclusion from the panel, exclusion from specific topic areas, or other actions were warranted. No individual was found to have a conflict of interest requiring exclusion from participation. Transparency was ensured by sharing details of each member’s associations with commercial organizations and potential intellectual conflicts with the group. The names and biographies of all GDG members were posted on WHO websites one month before the first GDG meeting, and no comments or observations were received. Key Questions The Steering Group developed key questions to guide the systematic review, using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes) format. These questions addressed leprosy diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. 1. Diagnosis: Questions focused on the availability of diagnostic tests with sufficient sensitivity and specificity for leprosy disease and latent leprosy infection, as well as their feasibility under programmatic conditions. 2. Treatment: Questions examined the effectiveness and safety of a single uniform treatment regimen compared to the currently recommended regimens for paucibacillary (PB) and multibacillary (MB) leprosy, as well as treatment options for patients with rifampicin resistance. 3. Prevention: Questions explored the effectiveness and safety of chemoprophylaxis and vaccines for leprosy prevention among contacts of leprosy patients and high-risk populations. Systematic Review Methods Systematic reviews were conducted by an independent reviewer commissioned by WHO, with oversight from the Steering Group and methodologist. Literature searches were performed using terms related to leprosy, diagnostic tests, antibiotic treatment, and vaccinations in databases such as Embase, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. For laboratory tests, inclusion was limited to studies published after 1996 due to advancements in laboratory techniques. Data extraction was conducted by the reviewer and Steering Group members, with the methodologist checking a random sample of extracted studies. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for intervention studies or the QUADAS-2 tool for diagnostic accuracy studies. Meta-analysis was not conducted due to the small number of studies, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity across studies. Cost-Effectiveness Analysis Cost-effectiveness was considered important for guideline development. However, for most PICO questions, no cost-effectiveness studies were identified, except for preventive treatment, where one study was reviewed and considered in formulating recommendations. Assessment of Evidence Quality The quality of evidence for each question was assessed using the GRADE method, modified for diagnostic tests. Evidence was categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low quality. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) started as high quality, while observational studies started as low quality but could provide reliable evidence for diagnostic accuracy. Evidence was downgraded based on risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision. Values, Preferences, and Ethical Considerations Values and preferences were considered to inform clinical and public health recommendations. Literature searches and an online survey were conducted to gather insights from individuals affected by leprosy. Focus group discussions were held in four countries (Colombia, Ghana, India, and Nepal) to explore perceptions related to diagnosis, treatment, and contact screening, as well as suggestions for improving service provision. A total of 70 individuals participated, including children, women, and men. Common themes included stigma, lack of involvement of affected individuals, and health system challenges. Suggestions were solicited to address these barriers and improve implementation of leprosy control services.
